To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) energetic masking leads to increased reliance on acoustic cues, whereas (b) informational masking leads to increased use of lexical-semantic knowledge.
energetic masking leads to a reduction of reliance on lexical-phonological information, while informational masking leads to a relative increase in reliance on lexical- phonological information.
energetic and informational masking lead to different effects on spoken word recognition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cognitive and neural mechanisms that support speech recognition in adverse listening conditions.
how listeners cope with adverse listening conditions, and how the brain manages the trade-off between bottom-up and top-down processes in speech recognition.
the question of whether the brain is able to recognize speech in adverse conditions, and if so, how.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of energetic and informational factors on the recognition of speech are different, but that both energetic and informational factors can be used in a similar way to reduce the processing load of the task at hand.
speech processing is influenced by both energetic and informational masking factors.
speech perception under a processing load is a function of both the energetic and the informational aspects of the load.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain uses a variety of strategies to cope with adverse listening environments.
the processing load can affect the way we recognize words, and that this effect depends on whether the load is informational or energetic.
speech processing under a cognitive load is more sensitive to informational than to energetic masking, whereas speech processing under an energetic load is more sensitive the other way around.
The main takeaway from our work is that
speech recognition in adverse environments is a complex, multifaceted process, which is influenced by the interplay between sensory, cognitive, and linguistic factors.
the study of the effects of processing load on spoken-word recognition can provide a unique window on the way in which speech recognition interacts with higher-order cognition.

speech recognition in adverse listening conditions is best described in terms of a trade-off between two distinct processes: one relying on acoustic detail and one relying on lexical-semantic information.
